facts.title: Named for its stench
facts.text: Bromine's name comes from the Greek word brômos, meaning stench. The pure element is a dense, dark reddish-brown liquid whose vapors have a sharp, choking, chlorine-like smell, which is exactly the property that inspired chemists to name it.

facts.title: A teenager's discovery
facts.text: Bromine was isolated in 1825-1826 by the young French chemist Antoine-Jérôme Balard, who was only in his early twenties at the time, while studying salty marsh water near Montpellier. The German chemist Carl Löwig independently prepared it around the same time, but Balard published first and is usually credited with the discovery.

facts.title: One of only two liquid elements
facts.text: At room temperature and standard pressure, bromine is one of only two elements that exist as a liquid; the other is the metal mercury. Bromine melts at about -7 degrees Celsius and boils at roughly 59 degrees Celsius, so it is liquid across normal indoor temperatures.

facts.title: It lives in the sea
facts.text: Bromine occurs in nature mainly as bromide ions dissolved in seawater, salt lakes, and underground brines rather than as the free element. The Dead Sea is exceptionally rich in it, and Israel, Jordan, the United States, and China are among the leading producers extracting bromine from such brines.

facts.title: The royal purple dye
facts.text: Long before bromine was identified as an element, its compounds colored the ancient world. Tyrian purple, the fabulously expensive dye worn by Roman emperors, is an organobromine compound (6,6'-dibromoindigo) produced by Murex sea snails, making bromine chemistry literally a mark of royalty.

facts.title: Flame retardant workhorse
facts.text: For decades, brominated compounds were among the most widely used flame retardants, added to plastics, electronics casings, and textiles to slow ignition. When heated, they release bromine radicals that interrupt the chemical chain reactions of combustion, although concerns about persistence and toxicity have since phased out several of these compounds.

facts.title: Once in every gas tank
facts.text: In the era of leaded gasoline, 1,2-dibromoethane was added as a 'lead scavenger' to keep engines clean by carrying lead away as volatile lead bromide. This was once a huge industrial use of bromine, but it largely vanished as leaded fuel was banned worldwide for health and environmental reasons.

facts.title: A guardian of the ozone layer's foe
facts.text: Atom for atom, bromine is far more destructive to stratospheric ozone than chlorine, by a factor often estimated near 45 to 60 times. Because of this, ozone-depleting bromine compounds such as halons (once used in fire extinguishers) and methyl bromide (a soil fumigant) have been heavily restricted under the Montreal Protocol.

facts.title: Maybe essential for life
facts.text: In 2014 researchers reported that bromine appears to be a genuinely essential trace element for animals, the 28th element known to be required. It plays a role in assembling collagen IV, a protein scaffold needed to build basement membranes, the thin tissue layers that support cells, suggesting bromide is not just an inert passenger in our bodies.

facts.title: The element that exposed photos
facts.text: Silver bromide was the light-sensitive heart of traditional photographic film and paper for over a century. When struck by light, tiny crystals of silver bromide form clusters of metallic silver that can be chemically developed into an image, a process that powered photography from the 1800s until the rise of digital cameras.
